title: The quasi-star model for Little Red Dots: potential and challenges
comment: Submitted to A&A. The catalogue with the best-fit parameters will be available upon acceptance. 12 pages (+ 4 in the appendix), 7 (+3) figures, 2 (+1) tables. Comments welcome
summary: (Abridged) Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a class of sources discovered by JWST observationally defined by a "V-shaped" rest-frame UV-Optical SED, a compact or unresolved morphology, and for having, frequently, broad hydrogen emission lines. Among various models, those involving a quasi-star interpret LRDs as an intermediate stage in the evolution of a super-massive black hole (SMBH) seed into a classic AGN. In this paper, we employ the radiative-transfer code \texttt{Cloudy} to study whether this model is able to reproduce the spectral features commonly observed in LRDs. The model consists of an accreting SMBH ($M_{\rm BH}\sim10^{5-6} \ M_\odot$) surrounded by a convective layer where a black-body (BB) spectrum with $T\sim5000 \ {\rm K}$ and $L\sim10^{44.4} \ {\rm erg \ s}^{-1}$ is produced. This BB is then reprocessed by a concentric thick ($ΔR\sim1000 \ {\rm AU}$) shell of dense ($n_{\rm H}\sim10^{11} \ {\rm cm}^{-3}$) gas partially ionised by thermal collisions. The emerging radiation is further reprocessed by a diffuse clumpy medium surrounding the quasi-star. We fit this model to JWST/NIRSpec spectra of LRDs from the literature, deriving the main physical parameters and the SMBH masses. Once coupled with the UV emission from a host galaxy, this model is able to reproduce the shape of the UV-to-NIR continuum, including the presence of a Balmer break, as well as the luminosity of the hydrogen emission lines. However, this quasi-star model does not natively account for the presence of broad helium lines and for the possible presence of hot dust, needing additional components to match these observables. Our main result is to show how some LRDs can be modeled as quasi-stars, highlighting that a significant degeneracy exists among different LRD models. This has important consequences for our understanding of the mechanisms driving black hole growth in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether quasi-star models (accreting SMBH seeds ~10^5-6 M☉ with convective envelopes and dense gas shells) can explain Little Red Dots (LRDs) observed by JWST. Using Cloudy radiative-transfer simulations, the authors find the model reproduces UV-to-NIR continua, Balmer breaks, and hydrogen line luminosities but fails to natively explain broad helium lines or hot dust, requiring additional components. The work highlights degeneracies among LRD models and implications for early black hole growth.
AI.motivation: To determine whether quasi-star models can reproduce the spectral features (V-shaped SED, broad emission lines, compact morphology) of Little Red Dots (LRDs), an enigmatic class of sources discovered by JWST, in order to understand whether LRDs represent an intermediate evolutionary stage between SMBH seeds and classical AGNs.
AI.method: The authors employ the radiative-transfer code Cloudy to model a quasi-star system: an accreting SMBH (M_BH ~ 10^5-6 M☉) surrounded by a convective layer producing a black-body spectrum (T~5000 K, L~10^44.4 erg/s), which is reprocessed by a thick (ΔR~1000 AU), dense (n_H~10^11 cm^-3) gas shell partially ionized by thermal collisions, and further reprocessed by a diffuse clumpy medium. The model is fitted to JWST/NIRSpec spectra of LRDs from the literature.
AI.result: The quasi-star model, when coupled with host galaxy UV emission, reproduces the UV-to-NIR continuum shape, Balmer break, and hydrogen line luminosities of LRDs. However, it does not natively account for broad helium lines or hot dust, requiring additional components. A significant degeneracy among different LRD models is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Some LRDs can be modeled as quasi-stars, but the model has limitations (no native broad He lines, no hot dust). The degeneracy among LRD models (quasi-stars vs. other interpretations) has important implications for understanding black hole growth mechanisms in the early Universe.

title: A Population of Red Galaxies with Very Strong Emission Lines at $z > 5$ Revealed by the NIRCam Medium Bands: ''Classic'' LRDs, Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies, and a Missing Population of LRDs
comment: 26 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The NIRCam medium-bands have proven to be efficient at identifying Emission Line Galaxies (ELGs) with high equivalent width (EW) H$α$ and [OIII]+H$β$ emission lines. In this paper we exploit this efficiency to identify a sample of ELGs at $4.9 \lesssim z \lesssim 8.9$ using medium-band imaging from the CANUCS, Technicolor, and JUMPS surveys. We find that the ELGs exhibit a strong correlation between continuum color and emission line strength, such that galaxies with bluer UV/optical continua have stronger H$α$ and [OIII]+H$β$ emission lines. We identify 26 galaxies that are outliers from this relation, which we call the Red Emission line Galaxies (REGs), because of their red continuum color and strong emission lines. We classify the REGs into three categories: 1) ''classic'' Little Red Dots (LRDs) selected with common literature criteria, 2) extended REGs, resolved in F444W and consistent with being Dusty Star Forming Galaxies (DSFGs), and 3) compact REGs, unresolved in F444W but not classified as LRDs. The compact REGs fail common LRD selections for several reasons, including faint continuua, contamination from emission lines (very strong [OIII]+H$β$), and UV/optical colors that are flatter than those of LRDs. We conclude that the compact REGs are likely LRDs that ''classic'' selection criteria miss, and are therefore missing from existing samples. Our results suggest that medium-band selection can provide more complete samples of these objects.

AI.tldr: Using NIRCam medium-band imaging from CANUCS, Technicolor, and JUMPS surveys, the authors identify emission line galaxies (ELGs) at z~4.9-8.9, find a strong continuum color–emission line strength correlation, and identify 26 outlier "Red Emission line Galaxies" (REGs) classified into classic LRDs, extended DSFGs, and compact REGs—the latter being missed by standard LRD selections due to faint continua, line contamination, or flatter colors.
AI.motivation: To leverage NIRCam medium-band efficiency in identifying high-equivalent-width ELGs and to uncover previously missed populations of red, emission-line objects (REGs) that evade traditional LRD selection criteria.
AI.method: Medium-band imaging selection of ELGs at 4.9≲z≲8.9 from CANUCS, Technicolor, and JUMPS surveys, followed by color–emission line correlation analysis and classification of outlier REGs into three categories based on morphology (F444W resolution) and LRD criteria.
AI.result: 26 REG outliers identified; classified into classic LRDs, extended REGs (DSFGs), and compact REGs. Compact REGs fail common LRD selections due to faint continua, strong [OIII]+Hβ line contamination, and flatter UV/optical colors.
AI.conclusion: Compact REGs are likely missed LRDs; medium-band selections can provide more complete samples of these objects than standard criteria.

title: The Combined Dense Gas and Excitation Atlas of the Milky Way I. Mass Distribution and Ripples in the Molecular Layer
comment: Submitted to ApJ, comments welcome! Main text: 13 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Appendices: 13 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
summary: The first components of a new meta-survey, the Combined Dense Gas and Excitation Atlas (CODEX) of the Milky Way, are presented here with combined data from five previously published surveys: NANTEN+CHaMP, ThrUMMS, FUGIN, and MWISP. The CODEX is first used to harmonise the combination of parameters used to describe the Galaxy's scale and rotation, including $R_0$ and $Θ_0$ from recent work, since these are critical components of standard techniques for obtaining kinematic distances. An additional feature is added to these formulae to accommodate local clouds that are otherwise kinematically inconsistent with the Local Standard of Rest. The structure in the combined lV diagram spanning 230 deg of longitude is then analysed, yielding a new Ragged Spiral Arm model that better traces the deprojected (x,y) 12CO structure. The widespread existence of ripples in the molecular layer, first reported in the ThrUMMS data of the Fourth Quadrant (4Q), is confirmed in FUGIN data of the First Quadrant (1Q), averaging amplitudes $\sim$40 and $\sim$23 pc respectively, and wavelength $\sim$4 kpc in both. The (x,y) mass distributions as traced by the molecular line data and the published dust extinction data match well across the 4Q+inner1Q, but poorly across the outer 1Q, probably due to lower sensitivity in the 1Q extinction data. In the 1Q+4Q, however, the two mean-z distributions do not match: the dust ripple amplitude is $\sim$3x smaller than, and opposite in sign to, the gas ripples. This is nevertheless consistent since the dust extinction is insensitive to the densest molecular gas.

AI.tldr: The CODEX meta-survey harmonizes five Milky Way surveys, creating a new spiral arm model and confirming molecular layer ripples (amplitude ~23-40 pc, wavelength ~4 kpc), while finding mismatches between gas and dust distributions due to dust extinction insensitivity to dense gas.
AI.motivation: To create a unified meta-survey (CODEX) combining five existing Milky Way surveys to harmonize parameters (R₀, Θ₀) for kinematic distances and to analyze large-scale structure in molecular gas distribution across 230° of longitude.
AI.method: Combined data from NANTEN+CHaMP, ThrUMMS, FUGIN, and MWISP surveys; harmonized Galactic rotation parameters; added accommodation for local clouds inconsistent with LSR; analyzed lV diagram; derived Ragged Spiral Arm model; compared gas and dust extinction distributions.
AI.result: Confirmed ripples in molecular layer in both 4Q (ThrUMMS) and 1Q (FUGIN) with amplitudes ~40 pc and ~23 pc respectively, wavelength ~4 kpc. Gas-dust (x,y) mass distributions match well in 4Q+inner1Q but poorly in outer 1Q. Mean-z distributions disagree: dust ripple amplitude ~3× smaller and opposite sign to gas ripples, consistent with dust extinction missing densest gas.
AI.conclusion: The CODEX meta-survey enables consistent analysis of Galactic structure; the molecular layer ripples are a widespread phenomenon; gas and dust trace different density regimes, explaining their vertical distribution mismatch.

title: The accretion history of the Milky Way V. The kinematics of most globular clusters trace the merger epochs
comment: A&A, accepted 1 June 2026, 7 pages, 3 figures, and Appendix A, B, C
summary: Several studies have associated globular clusters (GCs) with former Galactic accretion events by comparing their positions in the energy-angular momentum ($E$-$L_z$) plane, an approach further supported by similarities in their age-metallicity relations. However, recent merger simulations suggest that GCs initially associated with the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) disc may have lost their orbital energy and thus may not reliably trace this accretion event. We extend this framework by considering three N-body simulations of the Milky Way-GSE merger with different initial masses, mass ratios, and gas content. In addition to GCs belonging to the GSE disc progenitor, we accounted for GCs in its halo and, in gas-rich models, a population of GCs formed during the Milky Way-GSE merger. We confirm that most GCs originating in the disc have lost a significant part of their orbital energy during repeated passages through the dense disc medium, and we conjecture that associated tidal shocks may have destroyed many of them. In contrast, GCs from the halo and GCs formed during the merger have largely retained their orbital energy, which remains comparable to that of GSE stars even up to 9 Gyr after the completion of the merger. By using a more realistic GC population and GSE modelling, we find that most GCs linked to GSE can be associated with Milky Way accretion events in the $E$-$L_z$ plane, which supports previous observational associations based on a combination of energy-angular momentum and age-metallicity relations.

AI.tldr: Using N-body simulations of the Milky Way-GSE merger, the study shows that globular clusters (GCs) from the GSE disc progenitor lose significant orbital energy and may be destroyed, while halo GCs and those formed during the merger retain their energy. This supports the reliability of using the E-Lz plane to associate GCs with accretion events.
AI.motivation: To test whether globular clusters (GCs) can reliably trace past Galactic accretion events like GSE, given recent simulations suggesting GCs from the GSE disc may lose orbital energy and not preserve their original accretion signatures.
AI.method: Three N-body simulations of the Milky Way-GSE merger with varying initial masses, mass ratios, and gas content. The study tracks GCs from the GSE disc, GSE halo, and GCs formed during the merger, analyzing their orbital energy evolution in the E-Lz plane.
AI.result: Disc-origin GCs lost significant orbital energy and may have been destroyed by tidal shocks; halo and merger-formed GCs retained their orbital energy comparable to GSE stars even after 9 Gyr. Most GCs linked to GSE remain identifiable in the E-Lz plane.
AI.conclusion: Previous observational associations of GCs with GSE based on E-Lz and age-metallicity relations are supported, as most GSE-related GCs can still be reliably associated with this accretion event in the E-Lz plane.

title: Impact of fiducial cosmology in model-agnostic cosmological inference with the BAO feature
comment: 34 pages (17 + references and Appendices), 12 figures; prepared for submission to JCAP, associated code can be found at https://github.com/a-paranjape/zeldovich-smearing
summary: In recent work, we have developed a model-agnostic framework for cosmological inference using the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature in redshift space. The framework, which we dub the `Zel'dovich smearing approximation', involves several ingredients, including an optimal basis for the linear theory correlation function in real space, a Gaussian kernel that describes the smearing of the BAO feature due to bulk flows, and a model for the impact of scale dependent bias and mode coupling in redshift space. Unlike traditional, template-based approaches, this framework does not assume any particular cosmological model. An important ingredient -- which impacts both the traditional as well as model-agnostic frameworks -- is the geometric distortion introduced by the inevitable choice of the fiducial cosmology used for converting observed angles and distances to comoving separations. In this work we show how this distortion, which was not yet included in our framework, affects the output of the Zel'dovich smearing approximation. We test our completed framework on two halo samples derived from the $\texttt{AbacusSummit}$ simulation suite and designed to mimic galaxy samples from the ongoing DESI and Euclid surveys, respectively. We show that our framework produces unbiased cosmological constraints when applied to these semi-realistic samples and compare the organization of cosmological information in the model-agnostic and traditional approaches. We end with a roadmap to a detailed comparison of the performance of the traditional approach with the Zel'dovich smearing approximation, which is `data ready' as presented here.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Zel'dovich smearing approximation framework for model-agnostic cosmological inference using BAO, adds geometric distortion corrections from fiducial cosmology choices, validates on DESI/Euclid-like halo samples from AbacusSummit simulations, and demonstrates unbiased cosmological constraints.
AI.motivation: The previous version of the model-agnostic BAO inference framework (Zel'dovich smearing approximation) lacked inclusion of geometric distortions due to the fiducial cosmology used for converting observed angles/distances to comoving separations. This missing component needed to be addressed to produce a complete, data-ready framework.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) an optimal basis for linear theory correlation function in real space, (2) a Gaussian kernel for BAO smearing from bulk flows, (3) a model for scale-dependent bias and mode coupling in redshift space, and is now extended with geometric distortion corrections from fiducial cosmology. Validated on two AbacusSummit halo samples designed to mimic DESI and Euclid galaxy samples.
AI.result: The completed framework produces unbiased cosmological constraints when applied to semi-realistic halo samples mimicking DESI and Euclid surveys. The framework is now "data ready" for application to actual survey data.
AI.conclusion: The Zel'dovich smearing approximation is now complete with geometric distortion corrections included, and provides a model-agnostic alternative to traditional template-based BAO inference. The paper outlines a roadmap for detailed performance comparison between the traditional approach and this new framework.

title: JWST absorption line spectroscopy with SPURS: ISM covering fractions and kinematics in individual galaxies at $z=5-9$
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 31 pages, 18 figures, 4 Tables (including appendix). Comments welcome
summary: We present deep rest-ultraviolet (UV) spectra of six luminous $z=5$ -- 9 galaxies in the Abell-2744 field taken as part of the JWST Cycle 4 Large Program SPURS. The individual galaxy spectra show unambiguous detections of interstellar medium (ISM) metal absorption lines from low- and high-ionization states of enriched gas, which we use to probe the ISM gas porosity and kinematics. We find a striking diversity in the absorption profiles. We find low-ionization gas covering fractions ranging from 0.2 to 0.9, indicating a heterogeneous and patchy neutral ISM. The low-ionization kinematics also show a large diversity, with velocity centroid values ranging from $+$70 to a significantly blueshifted $-140$ km$\,$s$^{-1}$, while the high-ion gas shows mostly blueshifted absorption, indicating the presence of multiphase outflows. While all sources show outflow signatures in blueshifted wings, we also find that half of our sample, in particular those with the lowest stellar masses and highest sSFRs, have low-ionization velocity centroids close to systemic velocities. This is in contrast to near-ubiquitous bulk low-ionization gas outflows at lower redshifts. We suggest that this diversity of kinematics may be due to the bulk of the cold gas having low outflow velocities in the lowest mass and highest sSFR systems, potentially due to inefficient entrainment and/or an unresolved infalling component. These spectra reveal a metal-enriched ISM with complex gas geometry and kinematics, and highlight the potential of deep JWST grating spectroscopy to reveal the properties of the ISM during the reionization era.

AI.tldr: JWST SPURS program reveals diverse rest-UV absorption profiles in six z=5-9 galaxies, showing patchy neutral ISM (covering fractions 0.2-0.9) and multiphase outflows, with low-mass/high-sSFR systems showing minimal bulk outflow velocities, suggesting complex ISM gas geometry and kinematics during the reionization era.
AI.motivation: To probe the interstellar medium (ISM) properties — gas porosity, kinematics, and metal enrichment — in high-redshift (z=5-9) galaxies during the reionization era using deep rest-UV spectroscopy.
AI.method: Deep rest-UV JWST grating spectroscopy of six luminous z=5-9 galaxies in the Abell-2744 field as part of the Cycle 4 Large Program SPURS, measuring low- and high-ionization ISM metal absorption lines to quantify covering fractions and velocity centroids.
AI.result: Low-ionization gas covering fractions range 0.2-0.9 (patchy neutral ISM); velocity centroids span +70 to -140 km/s; high-ion gas shows mostly blueshifted absorption (multiphase outflows). Half the sample (lowest stellar mass, highest sSFR) have low-ionization centroids near systemic, contrasting with ubiquitous outflows at lower redshift.
AI.conclusion: The ISM in reionization-era galaxies is metal-enriched with complex, diverse gas geometry and kinematics; bulk cold gas outflows may be inefficient in low-mass, high-sSFR systems, and deep JWST spectroscopy is a powerful tool to reveal these properties.

title: The colour variability of low-z SNe Ia is entirely explained by dust
summary:
The relative importance of intrinsic colour variability of supernovae type Ia (SN Ia) versus dust-induced reddening remains an open question with important ramifications for understanding their environmental dependence, as well as for the validity of the traditionally employed Tripp linear correction for cosmological inference.
  We revisit this question in the light of two low-redshift, homogeneous datasets, the ZTF DR2 and Foundation DR1, which we analyse within the framework of the Bayesian hierarchical model Simple-BayeSN. We demonstrate both with simulation and on real data that traditional colour cuts, which remove highly reddened samples, induce a previously unrecognized selection effect, which may have biased previous conclusions on the origin of SN Ia colour variability. Once this is accounted for, we are able to explain the entirety of the colour--magnitude correlation as due to dust effects, with no need for an intrinsic colour correlation. This result is robust with respect to a host galaxy mass split and projected distance from the center of the host.
  Our findings imply that the traditional linear Tripp correction maintains an empirical validity, even though it should be ascribed to dust rather than intrinsic colour variation.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines whether SN Ia colour variability is intrinsic or due to dust, using ZTF DR2 and Foundation DR1 data with the Simple-BayeSN model. After accounting for selection effects from colour cuts, the colour-magnitude correlation is fully explained by dust, with no intrinsic colour correlation needed.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing debate on whether SN Ia colour variability is intrinsic or caused by dust, which has important implications for understanding environmental dependencies and the validity of the Tripp linear correction used in cosmological inference.
AI.method: Bayesian hierarchical modelling (Simple-BayeSN) applied to two low-redshift homogeneous datasets (ZTF DR1 and Foundation DR1), with simulation-based correction for selection effects induced by traditional colour cuts that remove highly reddened samples.
AI.result: Traditional colour cuts introduce a previously unrecognized selection effect that biased previous conclusions. After accounting for this, the entire colour-magnitude correlation is explained by dust effects alone, with no intrinsic colour correlation required. The result is robust to host galaxy mass split and projected distance.
AI.conclusion: The traditional linear Tripp correction remains empirically valid for cosmology, but should be interpreted as correcting for dust reddening rather than intrinsic colour variation.

title: The Pristine Dwarf Galaxy Survey -- VII. The metallicity distributions of 12 Milky Way faint satellites
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments are welcomed
summary: Spectroscopic studies of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are typically limited to small samples of stars due to the scarcity of sufficiently bright targets. The small number statistics and possible presence of contaminants still hamper solid determinations of their metallicity distribution function. In this work, we characterise the metallicity distributions of 12 Milky Way faint satellites by exploiting deep narrow-band CaHK photometry from the Pristine dwarf galaxy survey. In order to derive accurate stellar photometric metallicities, we combined it with deep broad-band g and r photometry from Muñoz et al. (2018) and Pan-STARRS1, covering each system out to 5-8 times their half-light radius Rh, and reaching magnitudes as faint as g~23. Membership probabilities were determined incorporating the available spatial, photometric, astrometric, and spectroscopic information, further refined using the derived photometric metallicities. We identified 3917 probable member stars across the 12 systems, more than doubling the numbers recovered by previous spectroscopic studies. We deliver complete metallicity distributions that yield robust average metallicities and dispersions previously inaccessible for most of the systems examined in this study. We identify 170 candidate extremely metal-poor stars distributed across all systems, and confirm a departure from the linear luminosity-metallicity relation in the ultra-faint regime, with systems scattering around [Fe/H]~-2.3 dex. Given the extensive mass coverage of our sample, we were able to investigate the presence of metallicity gradients, finding clear evidence of radial variations in massive systems, but none in the ultra-faint dwarfs within 2.5xRh. The photometric strategy presented in this paper will continue to serve as an effective complement to future spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: Using deep narrow-band CaHK photometry from the Pristine survey combined with broad-band g,r photometry, the authors characterize metallicity distributions of 12 Milky Way ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, identifying 3917 probable members (doubling previous samples), delivering robust average metallicities, finding 170 extremely metal-poor star candidates, confirming a departure from the linear luminosity-metallicity relation in the ultra-faint regime, and detecting metallicity gradients only in massive systems.
AI.motivation: Spectroscopic studies of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are limited to small samples due to scarcity of bright targets, and small-number statistics with contaminants hinder reliable determinations of their metallicity distribution functions.
AI.method: Deep narrow-band CaHK photometry from Pristine was combined with deep broad-band g,r photometry from Muñoz et al. (2018) and Pan-STARRS1. Membership probabilities were determined using spatial, photometric, astrometric, and spectroscopic information, further refined with photometric metallicities.
AI.result: Identified 3917 probable members across 12 systems (doubling previous spectroscopic samples), derived complete metallicity distributions, found 170 extremely metal-poor star candidates, confirmed departure from linear luminosity-metallicity relation in ultra-faint regime (~-2.3 dex), detected radial metallicity gradients in massive systems but none in ultra-faint dwarfs within 2.5×Rh.
AI.conclusion: The photometric strategy using CaHK narrow-band photometry effectively complements future spectroscopic surveys for characterizing ultra-faint dwarf galaxies.

title: Halo mass functions in mixed cold and fuzzy dark matter models
comment: 17 pages, 12 Figures, 1 Table, Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: We investigate the impact of mixed cold and fuzzy dark matter (MDM) cosmologies on the halo mass function (HMF) using numerical simulations performed with the AxiREPO framework. We consider models in which an ultralight axion-like component with mass $m =10^{-24.5} \mathrm{eV}$ constitutes a fraction $f \leq 0.3$ of the total dark matter. To enable consistent halo identification in mixed-species scenarios, we develop a grid-based halo-finding pipeline that combines the particle-based cold dark matter (CDM) and wave-like fuzzy dark matter (FDM) components into a unified density field. We find that FDM traces the large-scale CDM distribution while suppressing small-scale structure through wave interference effects, leading to a reduction in the abundance of low-mass haloes and modifying the HMF in a manner dependent on redshift and FDM fraction. Increasing the FDM fraction produces a systematic downward shift in the HMF and modifies its high-mass slope. Motivated by these trends, we introduce a phenomenological model that maps CDM HMFs to their MDM counterparts using a suppression function with parameters dependent on redshift and FDM fraction. This model reproduces the simulated HMFs within approximately 0.1 to 0.2 dex across the parameter space explored ($1 \leq z \leq 4$, $f \leq 0.3$). Our results provide a computationally efficient method for predicting structure formation in MDM cosmologies without requiring dedicated simulations for each parameter choice, and establish a framework for exploring the impact of MDM on cosmological structure formation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies mixed cold + fuzzy dark matter cosmologies using AxiREPO simulations, develops a grid-based halo finder for mixed-species dark matter, and proposes a phenomenological model that maps CDM halo mass functions to MDM counterparts via a suppression function, achieving ~0.1-0.2 dex accuracy for z≤4 and FDM fraction f≤0.3.
AI.motivation: To understand how a mixed dark matter scenario (CDM + ultralight axion-like FDM) affects the halo mass function, and to develop an efficient way to predict structure formation without running dedicated simulations for every parameter combination.
AI.method: Numerical simulations using the AxiREPO framework with FDM mass m=10^{-24.5} eV and fraction f≤0.3; a grid-based halo finder that unifies particle-based CDM and wave-based FDM into a single density field; a phenomenological suppression function model mapping CDM HMFs to MDM HMFs with redshift- and fraction-dependent parameters.
AI.result: FDM traces large-scale CDM while suppressing small-scale structure via wave interference; increasing FDM fraction systematically shifts the HMF downward and modifies the high-mass slope; the phenomenological model reproduces simulated HMFs within ~0.1-0.2 dex for 1≤z≤4 and f≤0.3.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model offers a computationally efficient tool for predicting MDM structure formation without case-by-case simulations, establishing a framework for further exploration of mixed dark matter cosmologies.

title: JWST reveals how black holes are fed: kiloparsec-scale multiphase filaments feed sub-kiloparsec circumnuclear disks
comment: Submitted to ApJ Letters and revised in response to referee comments (14 pages, 4 figures)
summary: The Centaurus cluster is one of the most important archetypes of radio-mode AGN feedback, with its central galaxy, NGC 4696, launching powerful jets that inflate X-ray cavities and regulate cooling and star formation. NGC 4696 lies within a spectacular multiphase nebula of filaments extending over tens of kiloparsecs and spanning six decades in temperature, from hot (10^8 K) X-ray-emitting plasma to cold molecular gas. Owing to its proximity, Hubble Space Telescope H_alpha imaging reveals a striking S-shaped ionized-gas swirl within the black hole's sphere of influence - the first such structure identified in a cluster core. Here we present the first JWST observations of NGC 4696 with NIRSpec, probing the inner 618 pc * 618 pc at 10 pc resolution. These data reveal that the ionized swirl is a rotating, multiphase circumnuclear disk (CND) physically and kinematically connected to the larger-scale filamentary network. This provides the long-sought missing link between kiloparsec-scale cooling flows and black hole accretion on <100 pc scales. Strikingly, the observed morphology and kinematics are reproduced by tailored magnetohydrodynamic simulations, in which filamentary gas condenses from the hot atmosphere, loses angular momentum, and feeds a rotating CND that mediates accretion onto the black hole. A similar structure in NGC 1275, the Perseus cluster's central galaxy, together with our results on NGC 4696 - two prototypical radio-mode AGN feedback systems - points to a common mechanism: multiphase filaments transport gas from cluster scales down to the vicinity of the black hole via a CND, closing the AGN feedback loop and establishing a physically grounded framework for self-regulated galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: JWST NIRSpec observations of NGC 4696 reveal a rotating, multiphase circumnuclear disk (CND) connecting kiloparsec-scale cooling filaments to black hole accretion, supported by MHD simulations, establishing a common feedback mechanism shared with NGC 1275.
AI.motivation: To find the missing link between large-scale (kiloparsec) cooling flows and black hole accretion (<100 pc scales) in radio-mode AGN feedback systems, using the Centaurus cluster's central galaxy NGC 4696 as a key archetype.
AI.method: JWST NIRSpec integral-field spectroscopy at 10 pc resolution covering the inner 618×618 pc region, combined with tailored magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to interpret morphology and kinematics.
AI.result: The previously known S-shaped ionized-gas swirl is identified as a rotating, multiphase circumnuclear disk (CND) that is physically and kinematically continuous with the larger filamentary network. MHD simulations reproduce the observed structure, showing filamentary gas condenses from the hot atmosphere, loses angular momentum, and feeds the CND, which mediates accretion onto the black hole.
AI.conclusion: A common feedback mechanism operates in both Centaurus (NGC 4696) and Perseus (NGC 1275) clusters: multiphase filaments transport gas from cluster scales to the black hole vicinity via a CND, closing the AGN feedback loop and providing a physically grounded framework for self-regulated galaxy evolution.

title: Inverse-Scattering Reconstruction of Inflation from Scalar and Tensor Primordial Spectra
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: We develop an inverse-scattering framework to reconstruct the effective inflationary potentials governing scalar and tensor perturbations. By recasting the Mukhanov--Sasaki equation as a Schrödinger-like problem on the half-line, we identify the Bunch--Davies initial condition with the asymptotic Jost solution and show that the freeze-out amplitude of the growing mode is encoded in the corresponding Jost function. This allows the scalar and tensor primordial power spectra to be written in terms of $F^{(s)}_{ν_s-\frac12}(k)$ and $F^{(t)}_{ν_t-\frac12}(k)$, respectively, and leads to an inverse-scattering expression for the tensor-to-scalar ratio as a ratio of Jost amplitudes. We then test the reconstruction in the large-$k$ regime using the Born approximation, where the Marchenko equation becomes linear. As benchmarks, we consider a smooth quadratic potential and a step potential that transiently violates slow roll and generates localized features in the primordial spectra. The reconstructed effective potentials reproduce the dominant behavior of $z^{\prime\prime}/z$ and $a^{\prime\prime}/a$ for smooth slow-roll evolution, while localized discrepancies arise in the scalar sector when sharp features induce stronger scattering. Our results show that inverse scattering provides a physically transparent method for connecting features in the primordial spectra to the underlying inflationary dynamics, and that the Jost function acts as a sensitive diagnostic of departures from canonical slow-roll evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an inverse-scattering framework to reconstruct inflationary potentials from primordial power spectra, using Jost functions to encode the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and tests the method on smooth and step-like potentials, finding good reconstruction for slow-roll but localized discrepancies when sharp features cause stronger scattering.
AI.motivation: To provide a physically transparent, inverse-scattering method for reconstructing inflationary potentials from observable primordial power spectra, avoiding the limitations of direct forward-modeling approaches.
AI.method: The Mukhanov–Sasaki equation is recast as a Schrödinger-like problem on the half-line, the Bunch–Davies initial condition is identified with the asymptotic Jost solution, and the primordial power spectra are expressed in terms of Jost functions $F^{(s)}_{\nu_s-1/2}(k)$ and $F^{(t)}_{\nu_t-1/2}(k)$. The tensor-to-scalar ratio becomes a ratio of Jost amplitudes. The Born approximation linearizes the Marchenko equation for large-$k$ reconstruction.
AI.result: Reconstructed effective potentials reproduce $z''/z$ and $a''/a$ for smooth slow-roll evolution. For a step potential causing transient slow-roll violation, localized discrepancies appear in the scalar sector due to stronger scattering from sharp features.
AI.conclusion: Inverse scattering provides a physically transparent method to connect features in primordial spectra to underlying inflationary dynamics, and the Jost function serves as a sensitive diagnostic of departures from canonical slow-roll evolution.

title: EPISODE II: Variability in the CO and H$_2$O rovibrational absorption lines in a periodically variable protostar EC 53
comment: Accepted in ApJ
summary: We present two-epoch JWST NIRSpec and MIRI observations of the young protostar EC 53 (V371 Ser), a periodically variable source with well-characterized quiescent and burst phases. The spectra in both epochs show absorption in the CO overtone ($\sim$2.3 $μ$m) and fundamental ($\sim$4.6 $μ$m) bands and the H$_2$O stretching ($\sim$2.7 $μ$m) and bending ($\sim$6.0 $μ$m) modes. We also obtained high-resolution ($R\approx45{,}000$) IGRINS spectra during the burst to constrain the CO overtone line profiles. LTE slab modeling yields gas temperatures of $\sim$1800 K (CO overtone) and $\sim$1200 K (CO fundamental), consistent with the overtone tracing hotter gas at smaller radii. The H$_2$O stretching-mode absorption shows no compelling evidence for variability, and the current JWST CO overtone data do not provide a robust constraint on overtone variability. In contrast, the CO fundamental and H$_2$O bending-mode features weaken by a factor of $\sim$2 during the burst, which is most naturally explained by continuum changes rather than large variations in absorbing gas. To quantify continuum dilution, we introduce a ``relative veiling'' that treats the quiescent spectrum as an internal reference and measures the change in the continuum excess between the two epochs. This formalism yields burst-to-quiescent hot-continuum ratios of $2.9\pm0.2$ for the CO overtone and $1.71\pm0.11$ for the CO fundamental. Using a viscous-disk prescription, these imply representative accretion-rate ratios of $\sim$3.6 and $\sim$2.0, respectively. The differing ratios suggest that inner-disk regions traced at different temperatures, and thus radii, respond differently across the burst cycle, consistent with episodic mass buildup in the inner disk during quiescence followed by more efficient transport through the innermost disk onto the protostar during the burst.

AI.tldr: JWST NIRSpec/MIRI and IGRINS observations of the young protostar EC 53 reveal absorption features from CO overtone (~2.3 µm), CO fundamental (~4.6 µm), and H₂O modes. CO fundamental and H₂O bending weaken ~2× during burst, attributed to continuum changes. A "relative veiling" formalism yields burst-to-quiescent hot-continuum ratios of 2.9±0.2 (CO overtone) and 1.71±0.11 (CO fundamental), implying accretion-rate ratios of ~3.6 and ~2.0, suggesting differential inner-disk response across the burst cycle.
AI.motivation: To understand how accretion bursts in young protostars modulate the inner-disk environment by using EC 53's well-characterized periodic variability as a natural laboratory.
AI.method: Two-epoch JWST NIRSpec/MIRI spectroscopy plus high-resolution IGRINS spectra, with LTE slab modeling of CO and H₂O absorption features, and a "relative veiling" formalism to quantify continuum changes between quiescent and burst phases.
AI.result: CO fundamental and H₂O bending-mode absorption weaken ~2× during burst due to continuum dilution; CO overtone shows no robust variability. Burst-to-quiescent continuum ratios of 2.9±0.2 (overtone) and 1.71±0.11 (fundamental) imply accretion-rate ratios of ~3.6 and ~2.0, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Different ratios across CO bands indicate that inner-disk regions at different temperatures/radii respond differently across the burst cycle, consistent with episodic mass buildup in the inner disk during quiescence followed by enhanced transport through the innermost disk during the burst.

title: From Cosmic Web to Supernova Remnants: Modeling FRB DM to Trace Baryons across Multiple Scales
comment: PhD thesis, The University of Osaka, 2026
summary:
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) provide a powerful probe of ionized baryons through their dispersion measures (DMs), but the observed signal contains contributions from the intergalactic medium (IGM), circumgalactic (CGM) gas, host galaxies, and source-local environments. In this thesis, I investigate FRB DMs from cosmic-web to source-local scales using cosmological simulations, zoom-in galaxy simulations, and supernova-remnant (SNR) simulations.
  Using the CROCODILE simulation suite, I study the DM-$z$ relation, baryon distribution, halo contributions, and host-galaxy DMs. AGN feedback redistributes baryons from halo centers into the diffuse CGM/IGM gas, particularly affecting DM contributions from massive foreground halos. From the simulated DM-$z$ relation, I derive diffuse baryon fractions of $f_{\rm diff}=0.865^{+0.101}_{-0.165}$ and $0.856^{+0.101}_{-0.162}$ for the fiducial and NoBH models. Host-galaxy DM contributions range from below 100 pc cm$^{-3}$ in dwarf galaxies to above 1300 pc cm$^{-3}$ in cluster environments.
  I also model young magnetars embedded in SNRs using one-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations. The dominant time-variable DM component arises from unshocked ejecta, while the shocked region contributes only a minor fraction. Comparisons with FRB 20190520B and FRB 20121102 suggest source-local DM contributions of tens to hundreds of pc cm$^{-3}$. Most models become transparent to GHz radio emission within 70 yr. In contrast, the shocked region dominates the RM contribution and evolution, with the $11\,M_\odot$ single-star model best reproducing the RM evolution of FRB 20121102.
  These results demonstrate that FRB dispersion measures must be interpreted as multi-component signals spanning a wide range of physical scales, linking the cosmic web, gaseous halos, host galaxies, and compact-object environments

AI.tldr: This thesis investigates FRB dispersion measures across cosmic-web to source-local scales using cosmological simulations, zoom-in galaxy simulations, and supernova-remnant simulations. It explores the DM-z relation, baryon distribution, host-galaxy contributions, and young magnetars embedded in SNRs, finding that FRB DMs are multi-component signals spanning wide physical scales.
AI.motivation: FRBs provide a powerful probe of ionized baryons through their dispersion measures, but observed signals contain contributions from multiple physical scales (IGM, CGM, host galaxies, source-local environments), which must be disentangled to accurately interpret FRB DMs and probe the cosmic baryon distribution.
AI.method: The author uses the CROCODILE cosmological simulation suite for studying DM-z relations and baryon distributions, zoom-in galaxy simulations for halo and host-galaxy contributions, and one-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of young magnetars embedded in supernova remnants for source-local DM and RM modeling. Comparisons with FRB 20190520B and FRB 20121102 are performed.
AI.result: AGN feedback redistributes baryons from halo centers, affecting foreground halo DM contributions. Diffuse baryon fractions derived are f_diff=0.865+0.101-0.165 (fiducial) and 0.856+0.101-0.162 (NoBH). Host-galaxy DMs range from <100 pc cm^-3 (dwarfs) to >1300 pc cm^-3 (clusters). Source-local DMs are tens to hundreds of pc cm^-3 from unshocked ejecta; most SNRs become transparent to GHz emission within ~70 yr. The shocked region dominates RM, with an 11 M_sun single-star model best reproducing FRB 20121102's RM evolution.
AI.conclusion: FRB dispersion measures must be interpreted as multi-component signals spanning a wide range of physical scales, linking the cosmic web, gaseous halos, host galaxies, and compact-object environments.

title: Star formation at z$\sim$0.9 from the OTELO survey: A comprehensive view combining deep optical spectroscopy and infrared data
comment: 15 pages, 13 figures
summary:
We aim to quantify the star formation rate (SFR) from deep optical spectroscopic data and far-infrared (FIR) photometry from a sample of galaxies at $z\sim 0.9$ from the OTELO survey and compare the activity estimated by optical tracers and FIR emission.
  We used the multi-wavelength OTELO catalogue to construct a sample of FIR sources. We identified and separated galaxies with active nuclei and derived the physical properties of the rest. We analysed their spectral energy distribution, obtaining estimates for stellar mass, dust attenuation, luminosity, and SFR based on infrared luminosity. We also studied H$β$ and [OIII] emission-line galaxies without significant FIR emission from previous works. This approach allowed us to perform a comparative analysis among the SFR obtained through different calibrators, in particular H$β$, presented in a previous work.
  We find that FIR-based SFR estimates uncover a significant fraction of hidden star formation. We determined that the SFR density obtained from the FIR emission is three times larger than that obtained from only emission-line sources. Likely related to the fact that each SFR tracer provides insight into star formation over different timescales, we suggest that such indicators are also more or less suited for different galaxy populations. Specifically, while optical emission lines effectively trace star formation in lower-mass galaxies, FIR-derived SFRs provide a more reliable measure in massive dust-rich systems. By accounting for both optically visible and obscured star formation, we provide a more comprehensive view of the star-forming main sequence at $z \sim 0.9$ and reinforce the importance of infrared tracers in studying galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: Using FIR and optical data from the OTELO survey at z~0.9, we find that FIR-based SFR estimates reveal three times more star formation than optical emission-line tracers alone, with optical lines better suited for low-mass galaxies and FIR tracers essential for massive dust-rich systems, providing a more complete view of the star-forming main sequence.
AI.motivation: To quantify SFR from deep optical spectroscopy and FIR photometry at z~0.9 using OTELO data, and to compare the activity estimated by optical tracers versus FIR emission, aiming to uncover hidden star formation not visible in optical bands.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength OTELO catalogue used to construct a FIR source sample; AGN identified and separated; SED analysis performed to derive stellar mass, dust attenuation, luminosity, and SFR from IR luminosity; Hβ and [OIII] emission-line galaxies without significant FIR emission from prior works analyzed; comparative analysis of SFR calibrators (especially Hβ) conducted.
AI.result: FIR-based SFR estimates uncover significant hidden star formation; SFR density from FIR is three times larger than from emission-line sources alone; optical lines trace star formation better in lower-mass galaxies, while FIR-derived SFRs are more reliable in massive dust-rich systems.
AI.conclusion: Each SFR tracer probes different timescales and is suited for different galaxy populations; accounting for both optically visible and obscured star formation provides a more comprehensive view of the star-forming main sequence at z~0.9, reinforcing the importance of infrared tracers in galaxy evolution studies.

title: Lyman-$α$ forest constraints on pure and mixed fuzzy dark matter
comment: 25 pages, and 8 figures
summary: Fuzzy dark matter (FDM), often realized as an ultralight scalar field, can suppress the growth of small-scale structures and could be strictly tested with Lyman-$α$ forest measurements. In this work, we constrain both pure and mixed FDM models (PFDM and MFDM) using measurements of the one-dimensional (1D) Lyman-$α$ forest flux power spectrum at $z=5.0$, 4.6, and 4.2. We perform cosmological hydrodynamical simulations with modified initial conditions and construct a two-stage neural network emulator for accurate analysis. The first stage predicts the cold dark matter (CDM) 1D flux power spectrum, while the second stage predicts the MFDM effect relative to the CDM baseline. This construction improves the sensitivity to weak FDM effects, enforces the correct CDM limit, and enables robust interpolation across a broad range of FDM masses and fractions. After marginalizing over the intergalactic medium parameters, we obtain the FDM mass $m_{\mathrm{FDM}}>1.9\times10^{-21}~\mathrm{eV}$ at 95\% credible level for the PFDM model. For the MFDM model, we find the FDM fraction of dark matter $f_{\mathrm{FDM}}<0.07$, $0.12$, and $0.65$ at 95\% credible level for $\log_{10}(m_{\mathrm{FDM}}/\mathrm{eV})=-23.0$, $-22.0$, and $-21.0$, respectively. When $\log_{10}(m_{\mathrm{FDM}}/\mathrm{eV})\gtrsim -20$, the current data do not provide an effective upper limit on $f_{\mathrm{FDM}}$.

AI.tldr: This paper constrains fuzzy dark matter (FDM) models using Lyman-α forest flux power spectrum at z=4.2-5.0 via hydrodynamical simulations and a two-stage neural network emulator, finding m_FDM > 1.9×10⁻²¹ eV for pure FDM and f_FDM < 0.07-0.65 for mixed FDM depending on mass.
AI.motivation: Fuzzy dark matter (ultralight scalar field) can suppress small-scale structure growth and requires strict testing with Lyman-α forest measurements to constrain both pure and mixed FDM models.
AI.method: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations with modified initial conditions were performed, coupled with a two-stage neural network emulator: Stage 1 predicts CDM 1D flux power spectrum; Stage 2 predicts MFDM effect relative to CDM baseline. This improves sensitivity to weak FDM effects and enforces correct CDM limit.
AI.result: Pure FDM: m_FDM > 1.9×10⁻²¹ eV at 95% CL. Mixed FDM: f_FDM < 0.07, 0.12, 0.65 at 95% CL for log10(m_FDM/eV) = -23.0, -22.0, -21.0 respectively. No effective upper limit on f_FDM for log10(m_FDM/eV) ≳ -20.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage emulator approach effectively constrains FDM models, providing competitive bounds on both FDM mass and fraction while marginalizing over IGM parameters.

title: Radiation Pressure Instability in the "turn-on" Changing-Look AGN SDSS J1430+2303
comment: submitted to apj. 16 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables
summary: We present a multi-wavelength study of the changing-look AGN SDSS J1430+2303. The optical flux increased by an order of magnitude over four years, driving a spectral transition from Seyfert 1.9 to 1.2. During the brightened high state, optical, UV, and X-ray light curves exhibited rapid decaying periods with progressively decreasing amplitudes. X-ray spectral analysis reveals a remarkably weak soft excess which declines more steeply than the hard X-rays as the total luminosity decreases. X-ray timing analysis shows a constant break frequency and a hard lag at $\sim 10^{-4}$ Hz during the luminosity decline, indicating a stable disk-corona geometry. Further broad-band spectral energy distribution fitting constrains the black hole mass to the range $M_{\rm BH}=4.7-19.5\times10^7\rm M_\odot$, corresponding to an Eddington ratio to $L/L_{\rm Edd}\sim0.024 - 0.046$, and favors a high spin ($a\gtrsim 0.86$). Consequently, we propose that the observed multi-wavelength decaying periods and damping amplitudes are associated with a shrinking unstable zone, driven by radiation pressure instabilities within the accretion disk.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength study of changing-look AGN SDSS J1430+2303 reveals a spectral transition from Seyfert 1.9 to 1.2, a weak soft X-ray excess, stable disk-corona geometry, and suggests radiation pressure instabilities in the accretion disk drive the observed variability.
AI.motivation: To investigate the multi-wavelength variability and physical mechanisms behind the changing-look transition in AGN SDSS J1430+2303, particularly focusing on the origin of decaying periods and damping amplitudes observed across optical, UV, and X-ray bands.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength light curve analysis (optical, UV, X-ray), X-ray spectral and timing analysis, broad-band SED fitting to constrain black hole mass, Eddington ratio, and spin.
AI.result: Optical flux increased 10× over 4 years (Seyfert 1.9→1.2); rapid decaying periods with decreasing amplitudes; weak soft X-ray excess declining steeply; constant break frequency and hard lag at ~10⁻⁴ Hz; M_BH = 4.7–19.5×10⁷ M⊙; Eddington ratio ~0.024–0.046; high spin a≳0.86.
AI.conclusion: The multi-wavelength decaying periods and damping amplitudes are likely driven by a shrinking unstable zone due to radiation pressure instabilities within the accretion disk.

title: Mass-Varying Neutrinos from an Inverse Symmetron
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures
summary: Neutrinos enter cosmology in different ways and are constrained by distinct observational probes across different epochs: as a relativistic species at high redshift, as a massive but clustering-suppressing component at low redshift, and as a particle physics observable in laboratory experiments. Low (verging on negative) bounds on neutrino mass from galaxy surveys motivate exploration of models where neutrinos may couple to dark energy, causing their mass to vary over cosmic evolution. If the coupling involves an inverse phase transition (symmetry broken, rather than restored, as neutrinos become nonrelativistic) this can tame instabilities in neutrino growth, appear as a lower neutrino mass in galaxy surveys, and add extra suppression to the matter power spectrum. We find that the late-time decoupling shuts down the fifth force and inhibits the excessive growth of neutrino perturbations, thereby eliminating linear-regime instabilities. The model may potentially address the Hubble tension via an early dark energy component localized around the time of recombination.

AI.tldr: This paper explores a model where neutrinos couple to dark energy via an inverse phase transition, causing their mass to vary cosmologically. This coupling suppresses instabilities in neutrino growth, mimics lower neutrino masses in galaxy surveys, and may help resolve the Hubble tension through early dark energy.
AI.motivation: Low (even negative) neutrino mass bounds from galaxy surveys motivate searching for models where neutrino mass varies over cosmic time, potentially explaining these observational anomalies.
AI.method: The authors propose a coupling between neutrinos and dark energy via an inverse phase transition (symmetry broken as neutrinos become nonrelativistic), and analyze its effects on neutrino perturbations, instabilities, and the matter power spectrum.
AI.result: Late-time decoupling shuts down the fifth force and inhibits excessive growth of neutrino perturbations, eliminating linear-regime instabilities. The model adds extra suppression to the matter power spectrum, mimicking lower neutrino masses in galaxy surveys.
AI.conclusion: The model resolves neutrino growth instabilities and may address the Hubble tension via an early dark energy component around recombination, while appearing as a lower neutrino mass in galaxy surveys.

title: Angular momentum evolution in the CIELO simulations. I. Temporal evolution of gas-stellar misalignments and baryonic merger timing
summary: Gas-stellar kinematic misalignments trace how galaxies assemble and reorient their angular momentum. Although well documented locally, their continuous evolution remains largely unexplored. We aim to characterise the pathways linking aligned, misaligned, and counter-rotating phases, assessing how gas accretion channels and mergers drive reorientation. We analysed 44 central galaxies from the CIELO simulations from z=3.5 to z=0. We defined kinematic episodes using the intrinsic angle, psi, between the star-forming (SF) gas and stellar angular momentum vectors, interpreting these histories by tracking accreted gas origins and evaluating paired statistical contrasts. Nearly 80% of the simulated galaxies are aligned at z=0, yet 86% experience at least one non-aligned episode. Although 19% of non-aligned episodes last >2 Gyr, their durations do not differ significantly from aligned episodes. Abrupt changes in psi coincide with intervals where accreted gas dominates the pre-existing SF reservoir and is highly tilted relative to pre-existing stars. During transitions, the median mass ratio of accreted to pre-existing SF gas rises from 0.57 to 2.14, and the median angular offset increases from 21.2 to 64.6 deg. While relevant mergers cluster near these boundaries, they can drive either alignment or misalignment regardless of mass ratios or orbits. Instead, mergers triggering abrupt transitions typically encounter hosts that are already partially decoupled. In the simulated sample, gas-stellar misalignment is fundamentally driven by reservoir competition. Mergers act as conditional triggers, but a galaxy's ultimate kinematic fate depends strictly on how newly accreted gas couples to, replaces, or mixes with the pre-existing material as it joins the central SF reservoir.

AI.tldr: Using CIELO simulations from z=3.5 to z=0, this study finds that 86% of central galaxies experience gas-stellar kinematic misalignment episodes, driven primarily by competition between accreted and pre-existing gas reservoirs, with mergers acting as conditional triggers rather than deterministic causes.
AI.motivation: To characterize the continuous evolutionary pathways connecting aligned, misaligned, and counter-rotating kinematic phases in galaxies, and to understand how gas accretion and mergers drive angular momentum reorientation over cosmic time.
AI.method: 44 central galaxies from CIELO simulations were analyzed from z=3.5 to z=0. Kinematic episodes defined by the intrinsic angle psi between star-forming gas and stellar angular momentum vectors. Gas accretion origins were tracked and paired statistical contrasts evaluated to interpret kinematic histories.
AI.result: 80% of simulated galaxies are aligned at z=0, but 86% experienced at least one non-aligned episode. 19% of non-aligned episodes last >2 Gyr. Abrupt psi changes occur when accreted gas dominates pre-existing SF gas (median mass ratio rises from 0.57 to 2.14) with high angular offsets (21.2° to 64.6°). Mergers cluster near transitions but can drive either alignment or misalignment regardless of mass ratios or orbits; mergers triggering transitions typically encounter partially decoupled hosts.
AI.conclusion: Gas-stellar misalignment is fundamentally driven by reservoir competition between accreted and pre-existing gas. Mergers are conditional triggers, but kinematic fate depends strictly on how newly accreted gas couples to, replaces, or mixes with pre-existing material in the central star-forming reservoir.

title: Towards Bayesian Photometric Cosmic Chronometers: Application to VIPERS
comment: 20 pages, 14 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: The cosmic chronometer (CC) method provides a direct measurement of the expansion history, $H(z)$, from the differential ages of passively evolving galaxies. However, most CC analyses rely on high-quality spectroscopy to select passive galaxies, measure age-sensitive spectral features, and control stellar-population systematics. We build on existing works that use the D4000 spectral break as a proxy for measuring galaxy ages and apply it to a photometry-selected galaxy sample from VIPERS PDR2 in the range $0.5 \le z \le 0.8$. Our goal is to extend the scope of the standard CC framework to photometric surveys. To achieve this, we first select a massive and passive galaxy sample using rest-frame colors and mass. Second, we design a Bayesian framework to infer full galaxy age posteriors in fine redshift bins, using a D4000-age-metallicity grid from stellar population synthesis (SPS) models. We also marginalize over metallicity, using a Gaussian metallicity prior to break the D4000-age-metallicity degeneracy. Subsequently, we derive age-difference posteriors between redshift bins by convolving their age posteriors to propagate the non-Gaussian features correctly. Finally, using the median and errors extracted from the differential age posteriors, we calculate the weighted average $H(z)$ over our selected redshift range. We obtain $H(z=0.65)=93.68\pm28.27\,{\rm (stat.)}\pm10.67\,{\rm (syst.)}\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, which is consistent with existing spectroscopic CC measurements and with the Planck $Λ$CDM prediction at the same redshift. This result provides a proof of concept for extending direct $H(z)$ measurements from cosmic chronometers to photometric and spectro-photometric surveys, where larger samples can compensate for lower spectral resolution, provided that passive-galaxy selection, metallicity priors, and stellar-population systematics are carefully controlled.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proof-of-concept for using photometric data (VIPERS PDR2) to measure the Hubble parameter H(z) via the cosmic chronometer method, using the D4000 spectral break as an age proxy. They obtain H(z=0.65)=93.68±28.27(stat.)±10.67(syst.) km/s/Mpc, consistent with spectroscopic CC and Planck ΛCDM predictions.
AI.motivation: To extend the cosmic chronometer framework from high-quality spectroscopy to photometric surveys, enabling larger galaxy samples to compensate for lower spectral resolution in measuring H(z).
AI.method: (1) Select massive, passive galaxies via rest-frame colors and mass cuts; (2) Build a Bayesian framework using a D4000-age-metallicity grid from SPS models; (3) Marginalize over metallicity with a Gaussian prior to break degeneracy; (4) Convolve age posteriors to derive differential age posteriors between redshift bins; (5) Compute weighted average H(z) from median and errors of differential ages.
AI.result: H(z=0.65)=93.68±28.27(stat.)±10.67(syst.) km/s/Mpc, consistent with spectroscopic CC measurements and Planck ΛCDM predictions.
AI.conclusion: Photometric CC measurements of H(z) are feasible provided careful control of passive-galaxy selection, metallicity priors, and stellar-population systematics. This opens the door to extending direct H(z) measurements to photometric and spectro-photometric surveys with larger samples.

title: Polarized and unpolarized synchrotron emission from dark matter in extragalactic targets
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures
summary: We compute 95% confidence-level upper limits on the dark matter annihilation cross section and decay rate from both total-intensity and polarized synchrotron emission in five extragalactic targets: M31, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), the Draco and Sculptor dwarf spheroidal galaxies, and the Coma cluster. Using Planck maps at 30, 44, and 70 GHz, we solve the diffusion-loss equation for dark-matter-produced electrons and positrons numerically with DRAGON and integrate the resulting synchrotron emission along the line of sight with HERMES, computing both total-intensity and polarized-intensity maps for each target with target-specific magnetic-field, gas, and radiation-field environments. The 30 GHz channel yields the most stringent constraints in all cases, and limits on annihilation or decay into $e^+e^-$ are stronger than those for $b\bar{b}$ due to the harder injected spectrum. For most targets the total-intensity and polarized limits are broadly comparable; the LMC is an exception, where Faraday depolarization in the turbulent disk suppresses the polarized signal relative to total intensity, making total intensity the primary estimator. Our results are robust against the choice of flux estimator and coordinate uncertainty. This work demonstrates that microwave polarimetry provides a complementary and largely independent probe of dark matter synchrotron emission in extragalactic targets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents 95% CL upper limits on dark matter annihilation cross section and decay rate using both total-intensity and polarized synchrotron emission from five extragalactic targets (M31, LMC, Draco, Sculptor, Coma cluster) using Planck 30, 44, and 70 GHz data, showing that polarized and total-intensity limits are broadly comparable except in the LMC where Faraday depolarization suppresses polarization, and demonstrating microwave polarimetry as a complementary probe of dark matter.
AI.motivation: To constrain dark matter annihilation/decay using synchrotron emission from extragalactic targets, and to demonstrate that polarized synchrotron emission provides a complementary and independent probe compared to traditional total-intensity analysis.
AI.method: Solve the diffusion-loss equation for dark-matter-produced electrons/positrons numerically with DRAGON, integrate synchrotron emission along the line of sight with HERMES, compute both total-intensity and polarized-intensity maps using Planck 30, 44, and 70 GHz data for five specific extragalactic targets with target-specific magnetic-field, gas, and radiation-field environments.
AI.result: 30 GHz channel provides the most stringent constraints; limits on $e^+e^-$ channel are stronger than $b\bar{b}$ due to harder injected spectrum; total-intensity and polarized limits are broadly comparable for most targets; LMC is an exception where Faraday depolarization suppresses polarized signal, making total intensity the primary estimator; results are robust against flux estimator choice and coordinate uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Microwave polarimetry is a complementary and largely independent probe of dark matter synchrotron emission in extragalactic targets.

title: Simple cyanides and formylium ions isotopologues in early star-forming molecular cores
comment: accepted in A&A (june 4, 2026)
summary: Understanding the chemistry related to the early stages of star formation is of great importance, as it is linked to the beginnings of the most complex chemistry in the interstellar medium. In this context, we investigate the chemical behaviour of simple cyano-bearing molecules and formylium ions isotopologues in a sample of massive infrared-quiet molecular cores. Using archive ALMA Band 7 data of 37 early molecular cores embedded in ATLASGAL clumps, we obtain abundances of HC$_{3}$N, H$^{13}$CN, HN$^{13}$C, H$^{13}$CO$^+$, and HC$^{17}$O$^+$. We used various statistical methods, including hierarchical clustering, to analyse the correlations between molecular abundances, ratios and temperature. We find that HN$^{13}$C, H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$, and HC$^{17}$O$^{+}$ abundances correlate positively with kinetic temperature, suggesting temperature-driven chemical regulation in young massive cores. A similar trend is observed for H$^{13}$CN, although the limited number of detections prevents a definitive conclusion. HC$_3$N abundances show no dependence on temperature within the 40-100 K range, suggesting a chemical steady state between gas-phase production and grain-surface depletion. Similarly, the H$^{13}$CN/HN$^{13}$C ratio, measured in only six regions, suggests no correlation with temperature, differing from findings at lower temperatures. Using a hierarchical clustering method based on abundance ratios, novel in astrochemistry, we identified chemically distinct core groups that align with thermal conditions. Additionally, we provide HC$^{17}$O$^+$ detections for 28 cores-a significant expansion of existing literature-and find evidence that H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ transitions may have higher optical depths than commonly assumed. These results are important because characterizing the chemical state of early star-forming stages is essential for understanding the onset of the most complex chemistry.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes ALMA Band 7 data of 37 massive infrared-quiet molecular cores to investigate the chemical behavior of simple cyano-bearing molecules and formylium ion isotopologues. Using statistical methods including hierarchical clustering, the authors find that HN¹³C, H¹³CO⁺, and HC¹⁷O⁺ abundances correlate positively with kinetic temperature, while HC₃N shows no temperature dependence. They identify chemically distinct core groups via clustering and significantly expand HC¹⁷O⁺ detections to 28 cores. The H¹³CO⁺ transitions may have higher optical depths than previously assumed.
AI.motivation: Understanding the chemistry of the earliest stages of star formation is critical because it is linked to the onset of the most complex interstellar chemistry. Characterizing the chemical state of massive young cores helps constrain the physical and chemical processes that govern star formation.
AI.method: The authors used archival ALMA Band 7 data of 37 massive infrared-quiet molecular cores embedded in ATLASGAL clumps. They derived abundances of HC₃N, H¹³CN, HN¹³C, H¹³CO⁺, and HC¹⁷O⁺. Statistical analyses included correlation tests and hierarchical clustering based on abundance ratios, a novel application in astrochemistry.
AI.result: HN¹³C, H¹³CO⁺, and HC¹⁷O⁺ abundances positively correlate with kinetic temperature; H¹³CN shows a similar trend but with limited detections. HC₃N abundances show no dependence on temperature (40–100 K). The H¹³CN/HN¹³C ratio (detected in only 6 regions) shows no correlation with temperature. HC¹⁷O⁺ was detected in 28 cores, significantly expanding literature. H¹³CO⁺ may have higher optical depths than commonly assumed.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate temperature-driven chemical regulation in young massive cores for several molecules, while HC₃N appears to have reached a chemical steady state between gas-phase production and grain-surface depletion. The hierarchical clustering method identifies chemically distinct core groups linked to thermal conditions. These results are important for understanding the earliest stages of complex interstellar chemistry.

title: Origin of monolithic high-z galaxies and UV luminosity of mergering high-z galaxies in the cosmological model with non-standard spectrum of density perturbations
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has detected an unexpectedly large number of galaxies at redshifts $z\geq 10$ compared to the predictions of the standard $Λ$CDM model. One of possible explanations is the presence of an excess (bump) in the power spectrum of perturbations at the mass scale of these galaxies, which is about $10^{10}M_\odot$. This excess simultaneously shifts the epoch of cosmic reionization to significantly earlier times, in contradiction with observations. Here we show that this defect of the bump model can be avoided if the perturbation spectrum has a cutoff (suppression) at smaller scales, which can be realized by lowering the amplitude of the primordial perturbation spectrum or by considering warm dark matter. With a cutoff present, fewer low-mass halos form and, consequently, fewer stars producing ionizing UV radiation. We also derive the halo merger-rate distribution in the presence of a bump using the extended Press--Schechter (EPS) theory, and verify this distribution against direct $N$-body simulations. Based on this distribution, and under the assumption that mergers trigger starbursts, we compute the UV luminosity function of early galaxies and demonstrate its agreement with available observational data. In the model under consideration, the fraction of early galaxies forming via the monolithic mechanism (through a single large-scale collapse) is significantly increased in comparison with the standard $Λ$CDM model, and the first stars appear directly in halos with masses $\geq10^8M_\odot$. We refer to such stars with primordial chemical composition as ``Population~IV stars,'' to distinguish them from the evolutionary different stellar populations.

AI.tldr: JWST detected excess high-redshift (z≥10) galaxies over ΛCDM predictions. A power spectrum bump at ~10¹⁰ M⊙ explains this but shifts cosmic reionization too early. This contradiction is resolved by adding a small-scale cutoff (via lower primordial amplitude or warm dark matter), reducing low-mass halos and UV production. Using EPS theory and N-body simulations, the model computes UV luminosity functions consistent with observations, boosts monolithic galaxy formation, and predicts first stars ("Population IV") form directly in ≥10⁸ M⊙ halos.
AI.motivation: JWST observations show an excess of z≥10 galaxies beyond standard ΛCDM predictions, motivating explanations such as a power spectrum bump at ~10¹⁰ M⊙. However, this bump alone causes overly early cosmic reionization, conflicting with data. The paper aims to resolve this contradiction.
AI.method: The authors introduce a cutoff (suppression) at small scales to the bump model, achieved either by lowering the primordial perturbation amplitude or invoking warm dark matter. They derive the halo merger-rate distribution using extended Press–Schechter (EPS) theory, validate it with N-body simulations, and compute the UV luminosity function under the assumption that mergers trigger starbursts.
AI.result: With the cutoff, fewer low-mass halos form, reducing ionizing UV radiation and avoiding overly early reionization. The UV luminosity function matches available observational data. The model increases the fraction of monolithic galaxy formation and shifts the formation of first stars to halos ≥10⁸ M⊙.
AI.conclusion: The bump+cutoff model successfully explains JWST's high-z galaxy excess without violating reionization constraints. It predicts a distinct "Population IV" stellar population forming directly in massive halos, differing from standard stellar evolution scenarios.

title: ALMAGAL IX. The chemical complexity of AG318.9477-00.1960: A line-identification template for ALMAGAL
comment: 21 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables
summary: We present a detailed molecular line analysis of one of the most chemically rich cores in the ALMAGAL sample, the high-mass core~9 in the AG318.9477-00.1960 clump (AG318-c9), located at a heliocentric distance of \sim 10.4\,\rm kpc. We further assessed whether the emission of selected COMs, that is, ethylene glycol ((CH_2OH)_2; EG), glycolaldehyde (CH_2(OH)CHO; GA), and methyl formate (CH_3OCHO; MF), can be used to trace the innermost regions of hot molecular cores (HMCs). We analysed ALMA Band~6 observations (\sim 217-221GHz). Spectral line identification and local thermodynamic equilibrium modelling were performed using the software MADCUBA. We derived the physical parameters, including the column density (N), excitation temperature (Tex), velocity, line width, and molecular abundances relative to H_2, for all detected species. The chemical inventory of AG318-c9 was compared with that of the HMC G31.41+0.31 (G31). In addition, we performed a pixel-by-pixel analysis of EG, GA, and MF to generate spatially resolved N and Tex maps and corresponding radial profiles.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the molecular inventory of the chemically rich high-mass core AG318-c9 using ALMA Band 6 observations, focusing on complex organic molecules (COMs) such as ethylene glycol, glycolaldehyde, and methyl formate. Through spectral line identification, LTE modeling, and pixel-by-pixel mapping, the study derives physical parameters and compares the chemical composition with the well-known hot molecular core G31.41+0.31.
AI.motivation: To assess whether emission from selected COMs (EG, GA, MF) can trace the innermost regions of hot molecular cores, and to characterize the chemical inventory of a chemically rich high-mass core in the ALMAGAL sample.
AI.method: ALMA Band 6 (~217-221 GHz) observations analyzed with MADCUBA for spectral line identification and local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) modeling. Physical parameters (column density, excitation temperature, velocity, line width, abundances) derived for all detected species. Comparative analysis with G31.41+0.31 and pixel-by-pixel mapping of EG, GA, and MF to produce spatially resolved N and Tex maps with radial profiles.
AI.result: Detailed molecular inventory of AG318-c9 with derived physical parameters. Comparison with G31.41+0.31 reveals similarities and differences in chemical composition. Spatially resolved maps and radial profiles of EG, GA, and MF indicate the potential of these COMs as tracers of inner HMC regions.
AI.conclusion: The selected COMs (EG, GA, MF) can serve as tracers of the innermost regions of hot molecular cores, and AG318-c9 exhibits a rich chemistry comparable to well-known HMCs like G31.41+0.31.

title: Dust in the very metal-poor galaxy Sextans A with JWST. I: Characterizing the evolved stellar population of Sextans A based on JWST observations and stellar evolution models
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The nearby star-forming dwarf galaxy Sextans A offers a unique window into galaxy evolution in the early Universe, owing to its extremely low metallicity (about 1-7% Zsun). Recent JWST imaging of Sextans A spanning 1-21 micron enables a detailed characterization of its dusty stellar populations and interstellar medium. In this work, we compare the observed JWST color-magnitude distributions of evolved stars with stellar evolution and dust-formation models to characterize the properties of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) population, including progenitor mass, formation epoch, metallicity, and dust production. Evolutionary tracks for 0.8-7 Msun stars with metallicity Z=10^-3 provide good agreement with the overall distribution of AGB stars in Sextans A. More than 90% of the AGB population occupies a nearly vertical sequence in the color-magnitude diagrams, corresponding to stars spanning a wide range of masses and ages but exhibiting little or no circumstellar dust. This sequence appears to be dominated by oxygen-rich (M-type) AGB stars and reveals that the F444W flux is a robust luminosity diagnostic. A small subset of sources displays strong infrared excesses and is dominated by carbon stars descending from 1.25-1.5 Msun progenitors that formed about 2-3 Gyr ago and are currently in the final AGB phases. Their MIRI colors imply very low metallicities, consistent with estimates from the red giant branch morphology (about 1-2% Zsun). Finally, we show that the JWST/NIRCam F277W-F444W color serves as an effective proxy for the dust production rate, with models predicting rates up to 10^-7 Msun/yr for the reddest sources in Sextans A.

AI.tldr: JWST 1-21 μm imaging of the ultra-low metallicity (1-7% Z☉) dwarf galaxy Sextans A reveals that >90% of its AGB stars form a dust-free, vertical sequence dominated by O-rich (M-type) stars, while a small carbon-star subset (1.25-1.5 M☉, ~2-3 Gyr old) shows strong infrared excesses and dust production rates up to 10⁻⁷ M☉/yr, with F277W-F444W color serving as an effective dust-production proxy.
AI.motivation: To characterize dusty stellar populations and AGB properties in an extremely low-metallicity environment (Sextans A, ~1-7% Z☉) as an analog for early-Universe galaxy evolution, leveraging JWST's unprecedented mid-infrared sensitivity.
AI.method: Comparison of JWST/NIRCam+MIRI color-magnitude distributions (1-21 μm) with stellar evolution and dust-formation models (0.8-7 M☉, Z=10⁻³) to constrain progenitor mass, age, metallicity, and dust production of AGB stars.
AI.result: (1) >90% of AGB stars form a dust-free vertical sequence dominated by O-rich M-type stars where F444W is a robust luminosity diagnostic; (2) a small subset with strong IR excesses are carbon stars (1.25-1.5 M☉, ~2-3 Gyr old) at ~1-2% Z☉; (3) F277W-F444W color predicts dust production rates up to 10⁻⁷ M☉/yr.
AI.conclusion: JWST resolves the AGB population in Sextans A at ultra-low metallicity, identifying a dominant dust-poor O-rich sequence and a minor carbon-star dusty component, with NIRCam colors serving as reliable dust-production diagnostics for low-metallicity systems.
